lines.text: Noise-cancelling headphones don't block noise. They add more sound, on purpose. So how does that make silence?
Sound is a wave of air pressure, pushing and pulling on your eardrum. A steady hum is just a wave that repeats.
A microphone on the outside hears that wave. A chip flips it upside down in a split second, and the speaker plays the mirror image.
Push meets pull, and they cancel. It's called destructive interference. Your eardrum feels almost nothing.
But the trick has a weakness. It needs a moment to react, so it works best on steady, low sounds, and struggles with sudden ones.
Quick test. Which does it cancel best? A, an engine drone. B, a dog bark. Or C, someone talking? Think!
The engine drone. It's steady and low, so the chip can predict it. A bark is sudden, and speech is fast and messy.
Two tips. Cancelling the noise lets you listen at a lower volume, which protects your hearing. And a snug fit matters, because physically blocking sound beats electronics for the high notes.
Watch again, and find the mirror image.
